pointers.sentence: Making a loader builds all of it, since `MigrationLoader.__init__` calls `build_graph` unless given `load=False` (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader`).

Each command of this chapter makes at least one: migrate through its executor, which hands the loader its own connection (`django/db/migrations/executor.py:MigrationExecutor.__init__`), the others directly.

A loader given `None` for its connection reads none: `build_graph` gives it an empty `applied_migrations` and sends no statement, and what it describes is the files alone. makemigrations makes the loader of `Command.handle` so (`django/core/management/commands/makemigrations.py:Command.handle`; [The makemigrations command](../makemigrations/makemigrations.md)), and so do squashmigrations and optimizemigration, the other two commands that write migration files.

`MigrationLoader.migrations_module` answers for a label with a pair: the dotted name of a module, and whether the setting `MIGRATION_MODULES` gave it (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.migrations_module`).
The setting is a dict by label, empty by default (`django/conf/global_settings.py`).

`MigrationLoader.load_disk` goes through the installed applications, imports the module that `migrations_module` names for each, and puts the label in one of two sets (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.load_disk`).

It imports each of the rest and requires one thing of it, an attribute `Migration`, which in a migration file is a subclass of Django's class of that name; a module without one raises `BadMigrationError` (`django/db/migrations/migration.py:Migration`).

`MigrationLoader.build_graph` calls `load_disk`, has the recorder read the applied migrations unless the loader has no connection ([What has been applied: `MigrationRecorder` and the table `"django_migrations"`](recorder.md)), and fills a new `MigrationGraph` in three passes over `disk_migrations`: the nodes, then the dependencies inside each application, then the rest (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.build_graph`).

The dependencies inside an application go in before those between applications so that a dependency on `"__first__"` finds the right root node (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.add_internal_dependencies`).

`MigrationLoader.add_internal_dependencies` adds an edge for each dependency that carries the migration's own label, but for one named `"__first__"`; `MigrationLoader.add_external_dependencies` takes the dependencies on other applications, each through `MigrationLoader.check_key`, and then `Migration.run_before` (`django/db/migrations/migration.py:Migration`).
It is given the dependency and the label of the application that asks, and returns a key, or `None` for a dependency to be dropped (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.check_key`).
The class's comment offers, as a use, a third-party application's migrations made to run after a project's replacement for the user model (`django/db/migrations/migration.py:Migration`).

`MigrationLoader.add_external_dependencies` passes each key through `check_key` and adds the edge with the migration named as the child and this one as its parent (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.add_external_dependencies`).

The connection is its argument, and it reads the rows with a recorder of its own, so a loader made with no connection can be asked (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.check_consistent_history`).
Django's documentation says that editing dependencies by hand can make such a history, and calls it a strong indication that they are incorrect (`docs/topics/migrations.txt`).
It returns a dict from each such label to the sorted names of its leaf nodes (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.detect_conflicts`).

`MigrationLoader.get_migration` takes a label and a whole name and returns the migration at that key in the graph's `MigrationGraph.nodes` (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.get_migration`).

`MigrationLoader.get_migration_by_prefix` takes the beginning of a name, as typed on a command line, and searches `disk_migrations`: one match is returned, several raise `AmbiguityError`, none raises `KeyError` (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.get_migration_by_prefix`).

`MigrationLoader.project_state` calls `MigrationGraph.make_state` and adds one thing to its arguments: the loader's `unmigrated_apps`, for the state's `ProjectState.real_apps`, an empty graph aside (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.project_state`; [The migration graph: `MigrationGraph`](graph.md)).

`MigrationLoader.collect_sql` is how sqlmigrate has a migration's statements without sending them: for each pair of a plan it opens a schema editor on the loader's connection with `collect_sql=True`, under which `BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor.execute` keeps each statement it is given and sends none, has the migration apply or unapply itself, and gathers what the editor kept, so a loader made with no connection cannot be asked (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.collect_sql`; [The migrate command, showmigrations and sqlmigrate](migrate.md)).
